01 / THE OPPORTUNITY

Every hospital visit starts
before the appointment.

Good clinical care deserves an arrival experience that is just as thoughtful. The first few minutes shape how confidently people move through the service.

01

Arrival uncertainty

Patients may not know where to check in, what to bring or what happens next.

02

Disconnected steps

Registration, queue numbers, signs and waiting areas can feel like separate systems.

03

Different needs

Children, guardians, older adults and disabled visitors need flexible guidance.

03 / DESK RESEARCH

Learning from hospitals
around the world.

A review of publicly documented patient-arrival services. We looked for practices worth carrying forward—and gaps worth exploring through design.

✳

The insight: self check-in is already common. The stronger opportunity is to connect it with what comes immediately after: reassurance, the right waiting area and support when a patient needs a person.

LOCAL LENS / NORTHERN FINLAND

Oulu matters, too.

Pohde's guidance for Oulu University Hospital (OYS) emergency services includes registration at an automated terminal. That confirms a locally relevant digital touchpoint—but emergency triage and planned outpatient visits are different services and would need separate safety research.

Pohde / OYS guidance ↗
FIFINLANDHUS / Helsinki

Registration with a card

HUS describes self-registration kiosks at hospital entrances using a Kela card, driver's licence or ID card, with reception alternatives.

DESIGN RESPONSE

Card scanning plus a prominent human-help fallback.

HUS guidance ↗
UKUNITED KINGDOMEast Kent NHS

Know where to go

East Kent Hospital kiosks use date of birth for self check-in and then direct visitors to their appointment location; staff remain available.

DESIGN RESPONSE

Put wayfinding directly after successful check-in.

NHS guidance ↗
USUNITED STATESCleveland Clinic

Flexible arrival methods

AppointmentPass supports a confirmation barcode or manual details, plus an attendant and front-desk fallback.

DESIGN RESPONSE

Multiple methods, one clearly visible exit to staff.

Clinic checklist ↗
SGSINGAPOREHealthHub

Queue before you arrive

HealthHub supports mobile pre-registration and queue-number collection during a location-dependent window before appointments.

DESIGN RESPONSE

Show queue status and connect a future mobile journey.

HealthHub FAQ ↗
AUAUSTRALIANSW Health

Wayfinding is a service

NSW Health publishes dedicated guidance for wayfinding across complex healthcare facilities, including arrival, signs and navigating change.

DESIGN RESPONSE

Consistent destination names, routes and physical signs.

Wayfinding guide ↗
IMPORTANT DISTINCTION

A Kela card is not a login.

It can support kiosk registration where the provider allows it, but it is not an identity document or proof of guardian authority. Production use must follow the hospital's identity and consent process.

Kela card information ↗
RESEARCH STATUS

Evidence, not invented outcomes.

This is a speculative, independent portfolio concept. Comparisons are public desk research—not usability studies, hospital partnerships, clinical validation or measured improvements.

Guardian authorization guidance ↗
04 / SERVICE DESIGN

One connected journey.
Not five disconnected screens.

The service blueprint aligns what the visitor sees with what staff and systems need to do behind the scenes.

SERVICE LAYER
01 Arrive
02 Identify
03 Confirm
04 Navigate
05 Reach care
PATIENT / FAMILY
Find kiosk; choose language
Scan card or QR
Review visit details
Follow printed/digital route
Wait in right zone
VISIBLE SERVICE
Welcome screen; calm cues
Large, clear entry methods
Accessible confirmation
Queue ticket and map
Staff and calling display
BEHIND THE SCENES
Kiosk availability / status
Provider-verified record lookup
Appointment validation
Clinic / route data
Queue management
SAFETY & SUPPORT
Accessible kiosk placement
Privacy and staff fallback
Guardian rules / exceptions
Step-free alternative
Help if destination changes

Proposed future-state service architecture. Systems integration and patient-safety workflows are not implemented in this prototype.

05 / DESIGN SYSTEM

Designed to feel
considerate, not clinical.

A small visual language built around legibility, steady guidance and an emotional tone that supports both adults and children.

Color & warmth

MIST#E4F2ED

Medical trust without an intimidating all-white palette. Color is always paired with labels.

Type & clarity

02 / TYPE
Care begins

Aa

Friendly, strong headings
DM Sans · readable interface text

Everyday interactions

03 / COMPONENTS
Large targets, short labels, clear feedback.

Touch-first buttons, generous spacing and an explicit path back or to human help.

A softer family mode

04 / CHARACTER
One step at a time.
We're here with you.

A gentle companion for child-facing moments—never a substitute for adult guidance or clinical communication.

06 / INCLUSIVE BY DESIGN

Good care includes
everyone.

Accessible digital service design is also physical service design: readable screens, clear routes, multilingual support and an easy way to reach staff.

Reference: WCAG 2.2 ↗
01

Clear and adjustable

Readable interface, large touch targets, larger-text and higher-contrast options.

02

Calm by default

No required motion. Reduced-motion preferences are respected; audio is never the only cue.

03

Language with dignity

Finnish, Swedish and English flows with simple, supportive wording.

04

Always a human option

Assistance, privacy protection and a staff handoff at each decision point.

07 / NEXT STEPS

Make arrival
feel like care.

The proposed next stage is to test the prototype with patients, guardians, hospital staff and accessibility specialists; validate privacy, guardian rules and emergency exceptions; then adapt it to a real facility's maps and appointment systems.
